answer: A healthy search shard only proves that the shard itself is serving queries; it does not prove that every message reached the index. In Discord's legacy search pipeline, messages first passed through a Redis-backed realtime indexing queue. When search-node failures caused a backlog, Redis could become CPU-saturated and begin dropping messages. Those messages never entered the indexing pipeline, so no shard, however healthy, ever contained them, and querying a healthy shard later could not recover documents that were never indexed. Two other mechanisms compounded the outage: a 50-message bulk batch could fan out across up to 50 nodes, so a single unavailable node failed the whole batch and forced all records to be retried, amplifying the backlog; and cluster-state/Lucene limits (master OOM raising the backlog, the roughly 2-billion-document MAX_DOC ceiling, and a restart-induced complete search outage) could deepen or prolong it. Discord later moved realtime indexing from Redis to a PubSub queue that can retain backlogs while Elasticsearch is unavailable and routed bulk writes by destination cluster/index, but the book notes that queue redelivery/idempotency, retention through prolonged outages, and a consistent index checkpoint still require separate validation. Queue retention alone therefore does not guarantee replay of every dropped message.
